title: ML Development Life Cycle (MLDLC)
abstract:
The nine stages of an end-to-end machine learning project, in order: frame the
problem, gather the data, preprocess, explore, engineer features, train and
select the model, deploy, test, and optimise. This document treats each stage as
a piece of engineering with concrete deliverables, exit criteria and failure
modes — not as a diagram to memorise. It also covers where the time really
goes, why the loop back from stage 9 to stage 1 is the whole point, and how the
remaining 75 topics of this course map onto the cycle.

blocks.t: The Cycle

blocks.cap:
The MLDLC. Stages 1–9 as given in the notes. The amber arrow is the
 part beginners ignore: this is a cycle, and a real project traverses it
 many times.

blocks.t: Why a life cycle exists at all

Machine learning is not "train a model". Training is one of nine stages and
consumes roughly a tenth of the effort. The MLDLC exists because the other eight
stages are where projects actually fail — and because each stage has an exit
criterion you can check before spending money on the next one.

blocks.cap:
Left: where the hours go on a typical project. Right: attrition —
 most projects that die do so before a model is ever trained, which is why
 stage 1 deserves disproportionate care.

blocks.t: Stage 1 — Frame the Problem
What this stage produces

A translation of a business problem into an ML problem, with an
agreed definition of success. Nothing is coded here.
The notes give the checklist explicitly:

head: Question
What you must actually settle
rows: "Predict which customers are about to churn from Netflix" — stated as a prediction with a subject, a horizon and an action attached to it
Supervised or unsupervised; regression, classification, clustering, anomaly detection, or ranking
What happens today — a business rule, a human analyst, or nothing. This is your baseline, and beating it is the bar
Does it exist, who owns it, how far back, can you legally use it
The business metric and the ML metric, and the mapping between them
Will the model retrain continuously or on a schedule (Topic 03)
Confirm with the people who will use the output that a prediction of this kind is actionable at all

blocks.t: The two definitions that sink projects

The target definition. "Churn" must become something computable:
cancelled within 30 days? Inactive 60 days? Failed to renew? Different choices
produce different datasets, different base rates and different models. Settle
this in writing.

The prediction horizon. "Will churn" is not a prediction until you
say when. Predicting churn one day ahead is easy and useless — nothing
can be done in a day. Predicting 30 days ahead is harder and actionable.
The actionability test

Ask: "when the model outputs a 0.83, what does somebody do differently?"
If there is no answer, stop. A prediction that changes no decision has no value
regardless of its accuracy.

Exit criterion: a one-page document stating the target variable, the
prediction horizon, the baseline, the ML metric, the business metric, and the
action taken on a positive prediction.
Stage 2 — Gathering the Data

Covered fully in Topic 10. The sources: CSV/Excel, JSON, SQL databases, APIs,
web scraping. In a real organisation this stage is dominated by access
negotiation and join logic, not by parsing.
The one technical decision that matters here

Split before you look. Hold out a test set at the very start, and do not
touch it again until stage 6 is finished. If you explore the full dataset, make
modelling choices informed by it, and only then split, your test set is
contaminated by your own decisions — a subtle form of leakage that no code
review catches.

Exit criterion: a reproducible script (not manual steps) that produces
a raw dataset from source, plus a held-out test set that has been set aside.
Stage 3 — Data Preprocessing
Turning raw data into something a library can accept. This is Topics 21–30.

items:
Remove duplicates — before splitting, or the same row lands on
 both sides.
Fix data types; parse dates into datetime (Topic 22).
Handle missing values (Topics 23–27).
Handle outliers (Topics 28–30).
Normalise inconsistent categories ("Mumbai" / "mumbai" / "BOM").
Handle mixed-type columns (Topic 21).

blocks.t: Fit on train, transform on both

Every statistic used in preprocessing — a mean for imputation, a min and max
for scaling, a category list for encoding — must be computed on the
training set only and then applied to the test set. The notes state this
repeatedly and it is the single most common source of optimistic metrics.
Stage 4 — Exploratory Data Analysis

Covered fully in Topic 11: basic questions (shape, head,
info, isnull().sum(), describe, duplicated,
corr), then univariate, bivariate and multivariate analysis, then
automated profiling.
EDA is not decoration

Every plot should change a decision. A right-skewed distribution tells you to
apply a log transform (Topic 18). Two features correlated at 0.97 tell you one
should go (multicollinearity, Topic 43). A bimodal target tells you there are two
populations and perhaps two models. If a chart changes nothing, do not make it.
Stage 5 — Feature Engineering & Selection

The whole of Part II, Topics 12–33. The four branches from Topic 12:
transformation, construction, selection, extraction.
Why this stage is where projects are won

Recall the Bayes error argument from Topic 05: no algorithm can extract
information that is not present in $X$. Changing XGBoost's max_depth
moves accuracy by a point; constructing the one feature that actually drives the
outcome moves it by ten.
Stage 6 — Model Training, Evaluation & Selection

head: Sub-step
What happens
rows: DummyClassifier / DummyRegressor, or the existing business rule. Everything is measured against this
Start simple. Linear/logistic $\to$ tree $\to$ random forest $\to$ gradient boosting. Complexity only when it is earned
$k$-fold on the training set to compare candidates without touching test (Topic 64)
Grid search, randomised search, or Optuna (Topics 64, 81) — tuned using validation folds, never test
Pick on the agreed metric, then confirm on the untouched test set once
Look at what it gets wrong. This usually sends you back to stage 5

blocks.t: The three-way split, and why validation exists

\underbrace{\text{Raw data}}_{100%} \longrightarrow 
 \underbrace{\text{Train}}_{\sim72%} + 
 \underbrace{\text{Validation}}_{\sim8%} + 
 \underbrace{\text{Test}}_{20%}
The notes are precise about the roles:

items: Training data — used to teach the model.

Validation data — a slice of the training data acting as a
 practice test before the exam. Model selection and hyperparameter
 tuning happen here.
Test data — touched once, at the very end.

blocks.t:
Why not select on test? Because selecting the model that scores best on
test means test has influenced training indirectly. After fifty
comparisons, the best test score is partly measuring luck, and your reported
number is optimistic. The test set is a single-use instrument.
Stage 7 — Model Deployment

Turning a trained object into a service. The concerns are the ones from
Challenge 8 (Topic 05): training/serving skew, latency, versioning, language
mismatch, feature availability at request time.

items:
Serialise the whole pipeline, not just the estimator — so
 serving applies the identical transformation.

Pin dependency versions. A pickle is not portable across
 library versions.

Choose the pattern: batch scoring into a table, a real-time
 REST/gRPC endpoint, or an embedded on-device model.

Ship a shadow deployment first — run the model on live traffic
 without acting on its output, and compare.

blocks.t: Stage 8 — Testing

Distinct from stage 6's evaluation. Stage 6 asks "is the model accurate?";
stage 8 asks "does the system work?"

head: Test type
What it catches
rows: Feature functions returning the wrong value on edge cases
Schema changes, new categories, out-of-range values, sudden nulls
The same input scored offline and online must give the same output
Latency and throughput at expected traffic
Whether the model improves the business metric causally — the only test that truly counts

blocks.t: Offline metrics do not prove business value

A model can improve AUC and reduce revenue — for example by recommending items
customers would have bought anyway. Only a controlled experiment measures the
causal effect. Budget for the A/B test in the project plan, not as an
afterthought.
Stage 9 — Optimise, and the Loop Back

items:
Monitor live performance, input distributions (PSI), and
 prediction distributions.
Detect drift (Topic 03) and decide the retraining cadence.
Retrain on fresh data; keep the ability to roll back.
Optimise cost — quantisation, distillation, caching, batching.
Feed error analysis back into stage 1 or 5.

blocks.t: The loop is the point

Version 1 exists to teach you what version 2 should be. Almost every large gain
in a mature ML system comes from a lap around the cycle — a re-framed target, a
new data source, a constructed feature — rather than from a better algorithm.
How the Rest of This Course Maps onto the Cycle
Code: The Cycle as a Script

"""End-to-end MLDLC skeleton. Every stage is labelled."""
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, joblib
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 1 -- FRAME THE PROBLEM  (written down, not coded)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Business problem : subscribers are leaving and we do not know which.
# ML problem       : binary classification.
# Target           : churned = no activity for 30 consecutive days,
#                    evaluated 30 days after the feature snapshot.
# Baseline         : current rule "flag anyone inactive 14 days" -> recall 0.31
# ML metric        : recall in the top decile of predicted risk
# Business metric  : retained revenue from the save-offer campaign
# Action           : top 5000 by risk get a retention call
# Online vs batch  : batch, retrained monthly
# =====================================================================

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 2 -- GATHER  (and SPLIT IMMEDIATELY, before looking at anything)
# =====================================================================
n = 8000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 60, n).astype(float),
    "monthly_spend": rng.lognormal(4, .6, n),
    "support_tickets": rng.poisson(1.2, n).astype(float),
    "plan": rng.choice(["basic", "standard", "premium"], n),
    "region": rng.choice(["north", "south", "east", "west"], n),
})
logit = (-0.05 * df.tenure_months + 0.4 * df.support_tickets
         - 0.01 * df.monthly_spend + 1.2)
df["churned"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .08, "monthly_spend"] = np.nan     # realistic gaps

X, y = df.drop(columns="churned"), df["churned"]
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
# X_te is now SEALED. Do not look at it again until stage 6 is finished.

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 3 + 4 -- PREPROCESS AND EXPLORE  (training data only!)
# =====================================================================
print("shape:", X_tr.shape)
print("missing:\n", X_tr.isna().mean().round(3))
print("target balance:", y_tr.mean().round(3))
print("numeric correlations:\n", X_tr.corr(numeric_only=True).round(2))
print("duplicates:", X_tr.duplicated().sum())

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 5 -- FEATURE ENGINEERING, inside a Pipeline so it cannot leak
# =====================================================================
num = ["tenure_months", "monthly_spend", "support_tickets"]
cat = ["plan", "region"]

pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("sc",  StandardScaler())]), num),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first"), cat),
])

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 6 -- BASELINE, CANDIDATES, CV, TUNING, then ONE test evaluation
# =====================================================================
dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy="stratified", random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("baseline AUC:", roc_auc_score(y_te, dummy.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]))

candidates = {
    "logistic": Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000,
                                                class_weight="balanced"))]),
    "forest":   Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(
                                                n_estimators=300,
                                                class_weight="balanced",
                                                random_state=0))]),
}
for name, pipe in candidates.items():                   # CV on TRAIN only
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:9s} cv auc {s.mean():.3f} +/- {s.std():.3f}")

grid = GridSearchCV(
    candidates["forest"],
    {"clf__max_depth": [4, 8, None], "clf__min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20]},
    cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("best params:", grid.best_params_, "cv auc:", round(grid.best_score_, 3))

best = grid.best_estimator_
prob = best.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]                   # <-- test touched ONCE
print("TEST auc:", round(roc_auc_score(y_te, prob), 3))
print(classification_report(y_te, (prob > .5).astype(int)))

# the metric the business actually asked for:
k = int(.10 * len(y_te))
top = np.argsort(-prob)[:k]
print(f"recall in top decile: {y_te.iloc[top].sum() / y_te.sum():.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 7 -- DEPLOY: serialise the WHOLE pipeline, not just the model
# =====================================================================
joblib.dump(best, "churn_v1.joblib")
# Serving applies the identical imputation, scaling and encoding.
# This is what makes training/serving skew structurally impossible.

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 8 -- TEST THE SYSTEM, not just the model
# =====================================================================
def validate_batch(batch: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    assert set(num + cat).issubset(batch.columns),      "schema drift"
    assert batch["tenure_months"].between(0, 600).all(), "impossible tenure"
    assert batch["monthly_spend"].isna().mean() < .30,   "upstream ETL broken"

validate_batch(X_te)

loaded = joblib.load("churn_v1.joblib")                 # training/serving skew test
assert np.allclose(loaded.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1], prob), "SKEW DETECTED"
print("skew test passed")

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 9 -- MONITOR, then loop back to stage 1 or 5
# =====================================================================
def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    cuts = np.percentile(expected.dropna(), np.linspace(0, 100, bins + 1))
    cuts[0], cuts[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected.dropna(), cuts)[0] / expected.notna().sum() + 1e-6
    a = np.histogram(actual.dropna(),   cuts)[0] / actual.notna().sum()   + 1e-6
    return float(((a - e) * np.log(a / e)).sum())

for c in num:
    v = psi(X_tr[c], X_te[c])
    print(f"PSI {c:16s} {v:.3f}", "<- RETRAIN" if v > .25 else "")
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
The nine stages: frame the problem, gather data, preprocess, EDA,
 feature engineering & selection, model training/evaluation/selection,
 deployment, testing, optimise.

Stage 1 has no code and decides the project. Settle the target
 definition, the prediction horizon, the baseline, both metrics, and the
 action taken on a prediction.

Split the data immediately and seal the test set. Fit every
 transformer on train only.

Train / validation / test: validation is the practice test, test is the
 exam and is used once.
Modelling is $\approx$10% of the effort. Data work is $\approx$60%.

Stage 8 testing is about the system — schema validation, skew
 tests, load tests, A/B tests — not about accuracy.

It is a cycle. The loop from 9 back to 1 is where the large
 gains come from.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Walk me through an ML project end to end.

Use the nine stages, and spend most of your answer on stages 1–5. Candidates who
jump straight to "I'd try XGBoost" signal that they have only done Kaggle,
where stages 1–3 are already done for them.
Q. Why do you need a validation set when you already have a test set?

Because choosing hyperparameters using the test set makes the test set part of
training. After many comparisons the best test score partly measures luck, and
the reported number is optimistic. Validation absorbs the selection; test stays
a clean, single-use estimate.
Q. When do you split the data?

As early as possible, before EDA. If you explore everything and then split, your
modelling decisions were informed by the test set — leakage that no code review
will detect.
Q. Your model beats the baseline by 2% AUC. Should you ship it?

Not automatically. Compare the value of 2% AUC against the lifetime cost:
serving infrastructure, monitoring, retraining, on-call. Then confirm the gain is
real with an A/B test, since offline AUC and business outcome are different
quantities.
Q. What is training/serving skew and how do you prevent it?

The transformation applied in production differs from the one applied in
training — a different imputation value, a different category ordering. Prevent
it structurally by serialising the entire fitted pipeline and using that single
object in both places, then assert equality of offline and online scores as a
deployment test.
